translations.text: Discourse of our holy and blessed father Basil on thanksgiving.
Behold, you have heard those words of the apostle, how he spoke to the Thessalonians and gave them a law for their whole life,
for his teaching was addressed to those people who came to him from time to time and from place to place.
But the benefit of his words extends to every race and to the whole life of humankind.
This, then, was the saying: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything."

But what that joy is, or what benefit comes from it, and how it is possible to accomplish unceasing prayer and to give thanks to God in everything, we will tell you a little later, according to our ability.
But now it is good that we first state what those opponents say who call these commandments of the apostle impossible, for they say:
What virtue is it to be in gladness day and night and in unquietness of soul?
Or how could this be accomplished, since countless are the trials and afflictions that befall us day by day,
which without doubt bring sorrow upon the soul, and in which joy and gladness are impossible,
just as it is not possible that someone should be burned and not feel the burning, or be wounded by a sword and not feel pain?
And perhaps here, even among us, one of those standing by is sick with this sickness and makes excuses for sins,
one who, because of his own negligence in keeping these commandments, lays the blame instead upon the lawgiver, as one who speaks of impossible things, and says:
How can I rejoice always, since the causes of joy are not in my power?
For the things that bring joy are outside and not within us, that is: the coming of friends,
being with parents, finding possessions, honors from people, return from sickness to health, and the rest of prosperity: a whole house full of good things,
a table always overflowing with delicacies, companions in joy, good things to hear and desirable things to see, the health of one's own people and the rest of their prosperity.
For distressing are not only those afflictions that come upon us alone, but also those that grieve our friends and afflict our relatives.
And when you have all these things, from them joy and gladness gather in the soul, and on top of all this,
that we should see the fall of enemies, the ruin of those who hate us, the honor of those who do good to us, and so, when we have nothing
and expect nothing distressing or disturbing to our life, then it is possible for joy to enter the soul.
How then has a command been given to us whose accomplishment does not come from our own will, but depends on other things that bring it about?
Or how can I pray unceasingly, since the needs of the body forcibly draw the mind to themselves, and it is impossible to divide the mind between two cares at once?
And again, giving thanks in everything has been commanded. But am I to give thanks when I am handed over to tortures, when I am beaten, or when I am bound upon a cartwheel?
Or if my eyes should grow dark and be cut off from me? Or am I to give thanks while I am being beaten and tormented by one who hates me?
Or if I should waste away from cold, or be choked by hunger?
Or when in a single moment I become childless, or am separated from my spouse by her death?
Or if by shipwreck at sea I am in a single moment reduced to poverty, stripped of all my wealth?
Or if I fall into the hands of robbers? Or if I am covered with wounds? Or if I am reviled by others? Or if they slander me?
Or if I become a beggar for bread because of my great poverty and do not have even a place to live? Or if I come to dwell in prison?
All this they say, and more than this, and they blame the lawgiver. And so they gather many words as an excuse for their sin, and they suppose
that they have found a worthy excuse, and they accuse the commandments of being impossible. But hear what we say in answer to all this:
that the apostle's view was directed toward another matter. He wished to raise our souls from the earth and lead them to the heavenly way of life, and for this reason he said all this.
But those who cannot reach that height of the lawgiver's mind, but move about in earth and flesh,
like worms in stench, also seek the force of the apostolic teachings in the passions of the flesh.
But he calls to everlasting joy not simply anyone who is full of passion, but the one who is
as he himself was, who no longer lives by the flesh, but has Christ living in himself,
and who, through union with the supreme good, no longer admits suffering together with the flesh on account of the afflictions that come upon it.

But even if the flesh is cut, the severing of the joined member remains in the suffering member of the flesh, and the grief of the afflicted body is unable to reach as far as the perceiving and rational soul.
For if, according to the word of the apostle, our members upon the earth are put to death, and we carry "the death of Jesus in our bodies," this is evident:

that the wounds of the flesh that has been made dead, being separated from its union with the soul, cannot reach it, and that bodily insults and afflictions and the deaths proper to the body cannot rise up to the mind,
nor can they bring down that height of the soul to the passions of the flesh, so that it should suffer along with them.
For if those who have fallen into afflictions are like that zealous man in mind, they do not bring him grief, since they themselves also bear without grief the things that have come upon them.
But if they are carnally disposed, even so they cannot distress him; rather, they are pitiable in his sight, not only because of their afflictions,
but even more because they do not know how to choose what is better. But why should I say much?
Let me say briefly that, in every respect, the soul that has once been nailed to longing for the Creator, and has been accustomed to shine with his beauty,
will not exchange its joy and gladness on account of the various changes of bodily afflictions,
but will make the very things that distress others a cause of greater joy, as the apostle Paul did.
For the weaknesses of the flesh, afflictions, persecutions and torments seemed pleasing to him, and he held all those deprivations as a boast,
as he was continually in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in persecutions and hardships.
Over the very things at which others grow faint-hearted and give up the hope of their life, over those he rejoices.
But those who are untaught, who do not know the apostle's purpose and cannot understand that he is calling us to the life of the Gospel,
these dare to accuse Paul, that great and lofty man, and say that he commands us to do impossible things.
But let such people learn that the causes of the joy that is fitting for us, ample and beyond words,
have been given to us by God, the generous giver: first, that we came from non-being into being, and then, that we were created in the image of God.
We have mind and reason, which bring our nature to perfection, through which we have come to know God, and we contemplate the beauty of created things skillfully and well, and through them,
as through a writing, we read the great providence and wisdom of God over all things.
We are able to understand good and evil; we have learned from our very nature to choose what is better and to turn away from what is harmful.
And on top of all this, we had become estranged from God through sin and were called back again to be his own;
by the blood of the only-begotten Son of God we were redeemed from that dishonorable slavery.
The hope of resurrection has been given to us, and existence among angelic good things, the kingdom of heaven, and the good things promised to us, which surpass every power of mind and speech.
Is all this not enough as a cause for unceasing joy and everlasting gladness?
Or the one who lives in gluttony and singing, who lies on a soft bed and has sleep as his occupation: shall we consider him worthy of joy?
But I say rather that for such people mourning is more fitting from all who have any sense, and that they should call blessed those
who, in the hope of eternal life, pass through the days of this life and with this passing affliction purchase those eternal and unpassing good things.
For even if they should be in fire, nailed fast to the love of God, like the three youths in Babylon,
or if they should be shut in with lions, or swallowed by a sea monster, we ought to call them blessed, and they too ought to be in joy,
so that they may not grieve over those passing afflictions, but may delight in the hope of the good things stored up for us.
For whoever has once entered the contest of virtue, that good contender, and has been stripped for the arena of godly service,
must bravely endure the blows of the opponents, in the hope of the glory of the crowns.
For even in earthly affairs, those who are accustomed to combat and its labors are not frightened by pain,
but they go with joy to grapple with the opponent, and through the desire and hope of victory and of wearing the crown they count the labor of a single moment as nothing.
In the same way, even if some hardship befalls the diligent servant of God, it cannot darken his joy,
for "tribulation produces patience, and patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope, and hope does not put to shame."
For this reason, in another place too, the same one commands us to have patience in tribulation and joy in hope, for it is hope that makes joy impossible to drive out of the soul of the diligent.
But again, the apostle himself commands us to weep with those who weep. And when he wrote to the Galatians, he wept for the enemies of the cross of Christ.
And what need is there to speak of the weeping of Jeremiah the prophet, and of Ezekiel's lament for the rulers by the command of God?
And you will find many of the saints who wailed, as one of them said: "Woe is me, mother! As what sort of man did you bear me?"
And another says: "Woe is me, for the careful man has perished from the earth, and there is no upright one among men!"
And another said: "Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at the harvest."
But search out thoroughly from the Scriptures the words of the righteous, and if you find any of them speaking in words of mourning, believe
that they all mourned because of this world and this passing and wretched life, as David said: "Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged."
For he longed to depart and to be with Christ, and he mourned the prolonging of his sojourn in this world, as something that ruins that joy.
And again, the same one uttered in a song that lament for his friend Jonathan, together with whom he also mourned for his enemy, as he said:
"I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan," and: "Daughters of Jerusalem, mourn over Saul," for he wailed for the latter as one who had died in sin,
but for Jonathan because he had been his companion in everything all the days of his life. And what need is there to speak of many others?
For he himself shed tears for Lazarus, and again he shed tears for Jerusalem, and he calls blessed those who mourn and weep.
And for this reason some say: How does all this agree with the word of the apostle, who said:
"Rejoice always"? For tears and joy are not of the same kind.
for in tears the soul is pierced as if by some wound, and is brought low by that unwelcome event, and the heart is constricted, and from this tears are born.
But joy is like a kind of leaping of the soul, which rejoices over the arrival of the things it desired.
For this reason they also differ in bodily appearance, for the complexion of the sorrowful is yellow and withered, while that of the joyful is
full of color and red and beautiful, when the soul, as it were, leaps and goes outward because of its delight.
But we say to them that the mourning and tears of the saints too were for the sake of the love of God,
for they always beheld that Beloved One with the mind and made the joy that comes from him grow within themselves, and
they provided for those fellow servants of theirs, and mourned for those who had sinned, and desired by means of tears to raise them up from their fall.
But just as those who stand on the seashore and pity those being tossed by the waves in it,
do no harm to their own firm standing through their concern over the others' drowning, so too those who grieve for their neighbor's sins
do not harm the joy of their own soul, but rather increase it, and through the tears they shed for a brother they become worthy of the joy of the Lord.
For this reason, blessed are those who weep and blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted and they shall laugh.
But by laughter he does not mean the sound produced in the cheeks and by the mouth from the boiling of the blood, but that gladness unmixed with any sorrow.
And again, the apostle commands us to weep with those who weep for this reason: such tears become like a seed and a loan toward that eternal joy.
But you, rise up in your mind and behold the life of the angels: is it anything else, and if so, what?
Nothing but everlasting joy and gladness, for they have been made worthy to stand before God and are filled with the beauty of the glory of our Creator.
And the apostle was drawing us toward such a life, and therefore he said, "Rejoice always."
As for the tears that the Lord shed over Lazarus and again over the city, I say this: he also ate and drank, not because he needed to.
Rather, he was showing you their proper and necessary use and its limit.
So it was also with his weeping: he shed tears in order to correct the passion of those who lament immoderately and improperly and who love mourning.
For like everything else, tears too are proper in their own measure, with regard to the matter over which, and for whom, tears are needed, and how much, and when, and how it is proper,
for those tears of the Lord were indicative of all this, and were not tears of passion.
And this is evident from what he said: "Lazarus, my friend, has fallen asleep, but I am going to awaken him."
But who among us would mourn over the sleep of his friend, whom he expected to wake after a short time, as He did when He commanded:
"Lazarus, come out"? And the dead man came to life, and the one who was bound walked.
Wonder upon wonder: the feet were bound, yet this did not prevent him from walking, for what gave him strength was greater than what hindered him.
How then could he who was about to do all this have judged the matter worthy of tears?
But it is clear that he bore our weakness in every respect, and with measure and limit he took on the necessary conditions of our nature, and from mercilessness,
as from a bestial thing, he kept far away, and likewise he turned aside love of mourning and immoderate mourning as something unrestrained.
And for this reason he wept over his friend and displayed his sharing in human nature, and he freed us from excess in both directions and taught us
that we should neither be drowned by grief nor be insensible to matters that call for grief.
For just as he took hunger upon himself when the solid food within him had been used up, and accepted thirst,
when the moisture of his body dried up and he grew thirsty again, when his joints and sinews were strained beyond measure by walking,
yet it was not that anything from that labor touched his divinity; rather, the nature of the flesh accepted the sufferings proper to it.
In the same way he also accepted tears, in order to show the working of the nature of the flesh, which comes about when the inner hollow of the head is filled with the vapors of grief, and then,
as through channels, by way of the passages of the eyes, it empties out the heaviness of such moisture.
For this reason too, certain roarings and whirlings and darkenings occur in the head as a result of unexpected griefs,
when the head is constricted by the vapors sent up by the heat that is in the depths of the body.
And then, I think, just as a cloud turns into rain, so the thickness of that vapor turns into tears.
For this reason too, a certain pleasure comes to mourners when they weep, for imperceptibly, through the tears, the heaviness of the head is relieved.
The truth of these words is shown by actual experience: for we have seen many who, having fallen into trials,
took it upon themselves to hold back their weeping, and afterward some of them came to madness or to paralysis of the limbs, and some even died.
For like a weak building, so their strength was crushed by the weight of that grief.
For just as a flame is smothered by its own smoke when the smoke has no outlet anywhere, so too, they say, it happens to the power in a person
that sustains his life: for it is destroyed and extinguished by grief when it finds no way out to the outside from anywhere.
So do not take the Lord's tears as a helper and witness for your own passion; for just as the food
that the Lord ate is not for us a pretext for gluttony, but rather for fasting and eating in moderation,
so too his tears were not a model of mourning, nor a law of lamentation, but a good and orderly measure and an excellent rule
of how one ought, honorably and in good order, and as befits the limit of nature, to bear distressing events.
For neither to women nor to men has such love of mourning and abundance of tears been commanded, but only
that they should be sorrowful over distressing events and shed a few tears, and these too in quietness and calm, and not with groaning and loud crying and lamentation,
nor with tearing of clothing, or pouring earth upon the head, nor with any other unseemly act such as is done by those untaught in such matters.
For it is right that one who has been purified by divine teaching should, as with a firm wall,
thus fence himself about with right reason, and should endure such distressing events bravely and patiently, and not,
as attackers easily break into a low, unwalled village, thus easily admit into his soul the multitude of passions.
For this is the act of a weak soul, one that has no strength at all from hope in God, that it should be undone by grief in so disorderly a way,
For just as worms are by nature born especially in soft wood, so griefs enter into weak souls.
If not, did Job perhaps have the nature and hardness of adamant? Were his heart and his loins perhaps made of stone?
When his ten children fell in a single moment, crushed by a single blow in the house of their rejoicing,
in that house of rest, when the devil brought the house down upon them, then he saw the table stained with the blood of his children;
he saw his children, born at different times, and departed from this life all together at one time.
He did not wail in a disorderly way, he did not tear his hair, nor did he speak any unfitting or weak word, but he offered that blessed thanksgiving, praised by all, and said:
"The Lord gave to me, and the Lord has taken from me; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; may the name of the Lord be blessed." Was that man perhaps merciless?
And how could that be? He who said of himself, "I wept over everyone in distress," was he perhaps lying in these words?
But the Truth itself bears witness to him that, along with his other virtues, he was also truthful, for it says:
"A man blameless, righteous, God-fearing, truthful and holy."
But you, O man, make your cry of mourning into a kind of melody, and with composed words, made for lamentation, you waste away your soul;
and just as singers have instruments to help their art, with which they proceed to sing, so you also suppose

that for mourners too it is becoming to have that melodic lament, and black clothing, and letting the hair grow, and darkness in the house, and that gloom, and pouring ashes on the head, and loud wailing,
so that in this way the wound of that grief may be continually renewed in your soul.
Leave all this to those who have no hope; but you have learned from Christ concerning those who have fallen asleep that:
"It is sown in corruption and is raised in incorruption; it is sown in weakness and is raised in power; it is sown a natural body and is raised a spiritual body."
Why then do you weep for him who has gone away to change his garment?
Nor should you weep for yourself, as though you had been deprived of some helper, for: "Better is hope in the Lord than hope in men."
Nor should you mourn for him, as though some evil had befallen him, for in only a little while the heavenly trumpet will awaken him, and you will see him standing before the throne of Christ.
So leave off those base cries of the uneducated, such as: "Woe is me, because of these unexpected evils!"
And: "Who would have expected these things?" And: "When would I ever have thought to bury my beloved in the earth?"
For at such things, even if we were to hear them from another person, it would befit us to be astonished,
we who, from the memory of things past and from the experience of present affairs, have learned those unavoidable facts of nature.
And if we teach ourselves by that word of truth, neither the untimely coming of death nor any other hardships will throw us into turmoil, as:
Look now: suppose I had a son, just come to the age of youth, the only heir of my life, the comfort of my old age,
the beauty of the family, the flower of his companions, the strength of the house, and such a one as this, in the very time of his excellence, were snatched away by death,
and had gone and become earth and dust, he who a little while before was sweet of speech and a desirable sight before the eyes of his parents. What, then, is it right for me to do?
Shall I tear my garment and roll on the ground and lament and show myself to those present like some child who is being beaten and cries out and thrashes about?
Or shall I call to mind and understand this nature of ours, and that the law of death cannot be evaded, and that it touches every age and separates all who are united?
And shall I not look on the matter as something strange, nor be stunned in my mind like one struck down by an unexpected wound, since I had learned from the beginning
that, just as I was mortal, so too the son I had was mortal, and that nothing human is firm and remains with its possessors forever?
Indeed, even cities great and glorious, adorned with the splendor of their buildings, the power of those who dwell there, and the other abundance of their commerce,
have been laid waste, and only in their ruins is there now a sign of their former glories. And again, a ship that has many times run across the sea and sailed swiftly, taking on countless cargoes,
vanishes at a single blast of wind. And armies many times victorious over their opponents, when their good fortune turns,
become pitiable both to see and to tell of. And nations and peoples of many tongues, many times, and mighty islands,
which had won many victories at sea and many on land, and had gathered great wealth of plunder,
either perished in the great length of time or were taken captive and acquired slavery in place of freedom. And why should I say much?
In short, whatever evil you name, you will find an example of it that has already happened in this life.
So then, just as we determine every weight by the accuracy of the balance, and discern the distinction of gold by rubbing it on the stone,
so too, when we consider every matter according to the measure given by the Lord and act accordingly, we shall never fall outside the boundary of right order.
For when something unexpected comes upon you, it will not be able to disturb you,
if you have taught your mind from the beginning not to be disturbed, and then also lighten that weight entirely by the hope of things to come.
For just as those whose eyes are weak do not wish to look at very bright things,
but rather rest their sight by gazing at flowers and greenery, so too the soul ought
not to sink continually into sorrows, but to lift itself up to the contemplation of those eternal good things.
Thus, then, you will be able to attain lasting joy, if your life always looks toward God and the hope of those good things lightens every sorrow for you.
Have you been reviled? Look to the glory that is being prepared for you through patience. Have you suffered the loss of some worldly thing?
Rather, look to the glory of heaven and to the treasure that will aid you through good deeds.
Have you been driven out of your homeland? But you have a homeland, if you strive to gain it: the heavenly Jerusalem. Have your children died?
Then strive, and there are angels with whom you will dwell around the throne of God, and you will rejoice with eternal joy.
In this way set against those passing afflictions the good things
that we await, and by this means keep your soul untroubled and undistressed, the state to which the command of the Apostle calls us.
Let neither the good things of human affairs bring immoderate joy into your soul, nor their sorrows bring its height low with grief.
For unless you have been taught in this way about this life and its affairs, you will never be free of agitation and trouble.
But you will accomplish this if you always keep as your constant companion the commandment that says:
"Rejoice always," and if you turn away sorrow over bodily affairs and gather in the joy of the soul, and count the good things of this world as nothing,
but let your mind always be in the hope of those eternal good things,
the mere remembrance of which is enough to fill the soul with joy and to establish angelic gladness in our souls through Christ Jesus
our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
